idiom_name: master role (partition/dispatch/combine) + N identical worker roles behind one sub-service interface
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one sub-service interface for a sub-task and its partial result; give the master three responsibilities - partition the request, dispatch sub-tasks (as call parameters, through a work pool, or into a repository the workers pull from), and combine the partial results; instantiate N semantically identical workers that own no shared mutable state. Decide up front whether sub-tasks are pushed with the invocation or pulled from a work pool (the workpool variant), whether workers operate on private copies or shared read-only data, and how results return (return values or a result repository). Sequence coordination phases in the master, never in the workers, and terminate with an explicit shutdown discipline (sentinels, completion counts, or cancellation). Keep the client unaware of the decomposition; that illusion is the point of the pattern.
code_sketch:
master:
  tasks = partition(request)                 # equal split or pull-based work pool
  for t in tasks: dispatch(t)                # call parameter, queue or repository
  parts = collect_all(tasks)                 # join / completeness count + timeouts
  result = combine(parts)                    # deterministic reduction or vote
worker:
  while (task = next_task()) != None:        # identical loop for every worker
      publish(process(task))                 # return value or result repository
pitfalls: Combining results before all sub-tasks are collected, or without a deterministic order, makes the outcome depend on scheduling.
Omitting the shutdown protocol (sentinels, completion count or cancellation) leaves workers blocked in next_task() forever.
Letting the master also process sub-tasks couples the coordinator to the work and turns it into the straggler.
